source_batch.unit_label: BFM Module C unit 1 (courseware unit 19): introduction to treasury management

facts.statement: Concept of Treasury (courseware): conventionally Treasury was confined to funds management: maintaining adequate cash balances to meet day-to-day requirements, deploying surplus funds from operations and sourcing funds for occasional cash flow gaps. In a bank it also meets the reserve requirements (the cash reserve ratio with the central bank and, to the extent required, investment in approved securities for the statutory liquidity ratio) and was seen as a service and compliance centre. After the economic reforms and deregulation of markets from the 1990s, Treasury has become a profit centre with proprietary trading and investment activity, accessing the markets for lending, borrowing, investing and trading in financial assets. Managing market risk for the whole bank has become an integral part of Treasury, which also plays an active role in asset-liability management (ALM) and is well placed to advise on internal pricing and strategy. Until the late 1990s investment in securities and foreign exchange were separate departments; they are now part of an integrated Treasury. Treasury essentially deals with short-term funds flow (under one year to maturity) except that some SLR securities are held beyond one year; risk management covers assets and liabilities across short, medium and long maturities.

Integrated Treasury and its driving forces (courseware): integrated Treasury means the integration of money market, securities market and foreign exchange operations, a result of financial sector reforms (deregulation of interest rates and partial convertibility of the rupee: freely convertible on current account and, to a large extent, on capital account). Banks can shift funds across currency markets to capture interest arbitrage, for example placing in rupee commercial paper against lending in dollars in the global inter-bank market, and can source funds from foreign currency accounts of residents and non-residents and external commercial borrowing of corporate customers. Rupee and foreign currency cash flows are no longer separate: an integrated cash flow is the basis of operations. Development of domestic equity and debt markets and settlement systems lets funds move easily from long to short-term or between currencies. Cash flow risk is common across currencies, and operating in many currencies and market segments creates currency and interest rate (price) risk, together market risk, so Treasury is involved in risk management and derivatives. Integration also brought Treasury into direct contact with corporate customers (merchant business) who now want an integrated service for hedging export receivables, raising foreign currency loans and overseas investments. The driving forces restated: integrated cash flow management, interest arbitrage, access to global resources, corporate demand for high-end services and risk management.

Functions of integrated Treasury and the three roles (courseware): meeting reserve requirements (CRR and SLR); global cash management; efficient merchant services (foreign exchange and advisory); optimising profit by encashing opportunities in the foreign exchange market, money market and securities market (debt, equity and credit derivatives); risk management of market risk; assisting ALM; and funds transfer pricing. Three roles: liquidity management (short, medium and long-term funds across currencies and complying with reserve requirements); proprietary positions (trading in currencies, securities and other instruments including derivatives to contribute to profits); and risk management (bridging asset-liability mismatches, providing derivative tools to manage risks in clients business and risks in its own proprietary positions). Treasury maintains three books: the ALM Book (internal risk management and traditional liquidity management), the Merchant Book (client-related currency and derivative transactions) and the Trading Book (trading in the markets).

Process of globalisation (courseware): globalisation is the process of integrating the domestic market with global markets, characterised by free capital flows and minimum regulatory intervention. Capital flows (in addition to the flow of foreign exchange on account of trade and remittances) include portfolio investment (foreign investors in domestic equity and debt), direct investment (long-term funds in projects, plants, outsourcing), external commercial borrowings, issue of equity or debt in global markets, mergers and acquisitions, and payments for technology, royalties and services. Inflows supplement domestic resources but sudden rise or fall in portfolio investment can raise volatility of stock prices, interest rates and exchange rates and expose the economy to systemic risks from other countries (the courseware cites the East Asian crisis of the late 1990s). Exchange controls have been progressively relaxed; foreign exchange transactions are permitted by automatic route through authorised dealers or by approval of the central bank, current account transactions are largely liberal, and most capital flows take place by automatic route, but full convertibility on capital account has not been permitted given the risks.

Impact of globalisation on treasury (courseware): the impact is three-fold. First, interest rates (central to lending, borrowing and investment) are influenced by global rates owing to cross-border flows, which also influence exchange rates; India has a managed float with minimum intervention, and in an open economy exchange rates are influenced by relative inflation, interest rates, GDP growth, stock markets and commodity prices. Second, new institutional structure: regulators, clearing and settlement institutions, depositories, credit information bureaus and credit rating agencies, plus primary dealers, mutual funds and investment institutions, have deepened the debt and equity markets and reduced counterparty risk; a payment and settlement system supports foreign exchange, money market and securities transactions. Third, rupee derivatives allowed in a phased manner: swaps, forwards and options for hedging and trading in currency and interest rates; equity derivatives are popular with investors but banks have not been permitted to use equity derivatives; and later products: currency and interest rate futures, credit default swaps on corporate bonds, cross currency futures and exchange-traded options. The specific dates, underlyings and limits stated in the courseware are not taught.

Treasury as profit centre: why and conventional sources (courseware): conventionally Treasury was a service centre with three markets handled in three departments (forex department for merchant business, investment department for assets, money market for cash flows); integration lets banks generate surpluses to supplement core banking profit. Profits are attractive because: Treasury largely operates in inter-bank markets with almost no credit risk and hence requires little capital allocation (although this has to be qualified by market risk capital, and institutional credit risk has become significant); the activity is highly leveraged so the return on capital can be high; operating costs are low compared with branch banking since a few specialist staff do high-value transactions (the courseware cites a minimum of Rs 50 million per transaction) in narrow spreads, so profit comes from high volume. Conventional sources: foreign exchange business (buy and sell rates for customers; the spread is profit; the bank squares the residual position in the inter-bank market on the same day; an overbought or oversold position at the end of day is an open position with exchange risk), money market deals (earlier mainly lending surplus funds and borrowing when required; the funds came from deposits at a cost above the money market rate, so a transfer pricing mechanism gives Treasury the cost of funds from branches) and investment activity (investing in government securities to meet SLR and little else; income from corporate debt and subsidiary investments was secondary until deregulation).

Contemporary treasury profits (courseware): profits now arise from market operations involving buying and selling, borrowing and lending or investing in tradable assets, taking a proprietary position. Sources: interest arbitrage (finding where interest differentials are in the bank favour across currency and security markets: borrow in USD and lend in rupee inter-bank, or the reverse, or borrow in the money market and invest in commercial paper or treasury bills; arbitrage between over-the-counter and futures markets); trading (a speculative activity with profit from price movements between buying and selling; currency trading within pre-set limits by banks holding an authorised dealer licence; trading in securities, mostly government securities which are liquid and traded on the wholesale debt market, bank treasuries holding more than the SLR requirement; equity trading is peripheral because the central bank restricts banks exposure to capital markets; credit instruments such as securitised paper, pass-through certificates and participation notes; single name credit default swaps); and treasury products (derivatives and structured products to corporate clients, such as a forward rate agreement to fix a rate on commercial paper to be issued after three months or a swap converting a floating rate dollar loan into fixed rupee interest, each with a built-in buy-sell spread in the bank favour). Treasury income is a significant part of gross income of scheduled commercial banks. It also supports transfer pricing: allocating the cost of funds to departments on a rational basis, adding the cost of hedging so profitability is more accurately known, with a small margin added to the Treasury profit for acting as funding centre. Banks also use risk adjusted return on capital (RAROC) pricing models.

Risk in trading and arbitrage example (courseware): while trading, treasuries incur market risk (loss when the exchange rate or the security price moves adversely), so they are subject to strict risk management controls. The courseware arbitrage example: a bank with surplus rupees could lend for seven days in the money market at 3.50 per cent. Alternatively the forex treasury does a buy/sell USD/INR swap for 7 days at a spot of 75.00 and forward 75.06, giving a premium of (0.06 / 75) x (365 / 7) = 4.17 per cent annualised; the dollars are placed abroad at 0.15 per cent, so the total return is 4.17 + 0.15 = 4.32 per cent, an arbitrage gain of 4.32 - 3.50 = 0.82 per cent (annualised) for seven days.

Organisation of Treasury (courseware): Treasury is organised as a department of the bank or as a specialised branch under the head office; the branch has its own books (P&L and general ledger), can act as authorised dealer in foreign exchange and participate in clearing and settlement systems, while a head office department can act only through a branch and has the advantage of easier coordination with head office departments. The specialised branch is the preferred form for integrated treasury. Treasury is headed by a senior person (a General Manager or Chief Treasury Officer or similar) reporting to the chief financial officer or chief executive, with reporting and delegation depending on bank size. It is divided into three main divisions: the dealing room (front office), the back office (treasury administration) and the mid-office (risk management), plus an investment department for primary issues and administrative departments (accounts, systems, remittances).

Front office, back office, mid office (courseware): the dealing room is headed by a Chief Dealer; dealers specialise in a market (foreign exchange, money market, securities) and, in an integrated treasury, are generally familiar with all; there may be dealers for merchant (customer) business and an ALM desk. The securities market is divided into primary and secondary, with dealing in government securities by dealers and participation in primary auctions on behalf of the bank; some banks have an equity dealer. The front office only executes deals and has no part in settlement. The back office verifies and settles deals from deal slips prepared by dealers and from confirmations received independently from counterparties, maintains and reconciles nostro accounts (foreign currency accounts with correspondent banks), funding and security accounts with the central bank and demat accounts, ensures margin money with the clearing corporation, and does book-keeping and periodic returns; settlement on value date is a key function and delay leads to reputational loss or default. Front and back office must be totally segregated and report to two different managers. The mid-office provides management information, implements risk management (exposure limits and stop-loss limits, monitoring of Treasury key parameters, transfer pricing mechanism); in smaller banks it may also function as ALM support. As per central bank guidelines, the mid-office should have market risk experts, economists, statisticians and general bankers, should be functionally independent, reporting to the ALCO, separate from the Treasury Department and not involved in day-to-day management; in most banks it reports to the Head of Risk Management so that compliance is objective. The investment department handles primary issues of corporate debt: appraisal of credit risk and documentation are needed, so it sits outside the dealing room; proposals are considered by an investment committee (courseware: minimum marketable investment Rs 5 crore).

payload.title: The concept of Treasury
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Traditional Treasury** was a **funds management** function: keep **adequate cash balances**, **deploy surplus funds**, **source funds to bridge gaps**, and meet **reserve requirements** (the **CRR** with the central bank and, as required, **SLR** securities). It was seen as a **service and compliance centre**.

Since the **1990s reforms and deregulation**, Treasury has also become a **profit centre** with **proprietary trading and investment**, accessing markets to **lend, borrow, invest and trade**.

- **Market risk** for the whole bank is now managed by Treasury.
- It plays an active role in **asset-liability management (ALM)** and advises on **internal pricing and strategy**.
- **Investment in securities** and **foreign exchange** were once separate departments; they are now part of an **integrated Treasury**.
- Treasury mainly handles **short-term funds flow (under one year)**, though some SLR securities are held longer; **risk management** covers **all maturities**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve compliance remains a core duty even as profit-making has grown.

self_check.prompt_text: What was the traditional role of bank Treasury?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Funds management: keeping adequate cash, deploying surplus funds, bridging gaps and meeting reserve requirements.

payload.title: Integrated Treasury and why it emerged
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Integrated Treasury** joins the **money market, securities market and foreign exchange** operations. It followed **financial sector reforms**: **deregulated interest rates** and a **rupee that is convertible on current account** and, to a large extent, capital account.

**Why it matters:**

- Banks can shift funds across **currency markets** for **interest arbitrage** (for example placing in rupee commercial paper while lending dollars in the global inter-bank market).
- **Rupee and foreign currency cash flows are no longer separate**: one **integrated cash flow** is the basis.
- **Developed domestic markets and settlement systems** let funds move **between long and short term** or **between currencies**.
- Trading in many currencies creates **currency and interest rate risk**, together **market risk**, so Treasury runs **risk management and derivatives**.
- Corporates now deal with Treasury directly for **hedging export receivables**, **foreign currency loans** and **overseas investment** (**merchant business**).

**Driving forces:** **integrated cash flow management**, **interest arbitrage**, **access to global resources**, **corporate demand for high-end services**, **risk management**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Integration turns separate currency desks into one view of cash and risk.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Treasury transactions with customers, as distinct from the bank own trading and investment business.

payload.title: Globalisation and capital flows
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Globalisation** is the **integration of the domestic market with global markets**, with **free capital flows** and **minimum regulatory intervention**.

**Forms of capital flow:** **portfolio investment** (equity and debt), **direct investment** (plants, projects, outsourcing), **external commercial borrowings**, **equity or debt issued in global markets**, **mergers and acquisitions**, and **payments for technology, royalties and services**.

**Benefits and risks:** inflows **supplement domestic resources**, but **sudden swings in portfolio flows** can raise **volatility** of share prices, interest rates and exchange rates and bring **systemic risk** from other countries (the late 1990s East Asian crisis is the courseware example).

**Controls in India (principles):** foreign exchange transactions go by **automatic route through authorised dealers** or by **approval of the central bank**; **current account** is largely liberal and most **capital** flows are by automatic route, but **full capital account convertibility is not permitted**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Capital account openness is kept partial because unrestricted flows can destabilise the economy.

self_check.expected_takeaway: For example portfolio investment and direct investment.

payload.title: Impact of globalisation on treasury activity
payload.core_explanation_md:
**First: interest and exchange rates.** Domestic rates are influenced by **global rates** through **cross-border flows**; these flows also affect exchange rates. India has a **managed float**; in an open economy the exchange rate also depends on **relative inflation, interest rates, GDP growth, stock markets and commodity prices**.

**Second: new institutional structure.** **Regulators, clearing and settlement bodies, depositories, credit information bureaus and rating agencies**, plus **primary dealers, mutual funds and institutions**, **deepen markets** and **reduce counterparty risk**.

**Third: derivatives.** **Rupee derivatives** (**swaps, forwards, options**) were allowed in phases; later **currency and interest rate futures, credit default swaps** and **exchange-traded options**. **Equity derivatives** are popular with investors but **banks have not been permitted** to use them (courseware). Dates and limits are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Derivatives let Treasury hedge as well as trade.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Global influence on interest and exchange rates, new institutional structure and rupee derivatives.

payload.title: Treasury as a profit centre: reasons and conventional sources
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why Treasury profits are attractive:**

1. It operates in **inter-bank markets** with **almost no credit risk**, so it needs **little capital** (though **market risk** capital still applies and **institutional credit risk** has become significant).
2. It is **highly leveraged**, so the **return on capital** can be high.
3. **Operating costs are low**: **few specialist staff** do **high-value** deals in **narrow spreads**, so profit comes from **volume**.

**Conventional sources of profit:**

| Source | How it earns |
| --- | --- |
| **Foreign exchange business** | **Buy-sell spread** to customers; residual position **squared in the inter-bank market**; an **overbought or oversold (open) position** at day end carries **exchange risk** |
| **Money market deals** | Earlier **lending surplus** and **borrowing as needed**; a **transfer pricing mechanism** gives Treasury its **cost of funds** from branches |
| **Investment** | Mostly **government securities for SLR**; other investments were secondary |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Low capital and high turnover give a high return on capital but not zero risk.

self_check.expected_takeaway: A residual overbought or oversold foreign currency position left at the end of the day, which carries exchange risk.

payload.core_explanation_md:
Profits now come from **market operations with a proprietary position**:

| **Interest arbitrage** | Exploit **interest differentials** across currency and security markets (borrow USD and lend rupees, or the reverse; borrow in money market and invest in **commercial paper or T-bills**; arbitrage between **OTC and futures** markets) |
| **Trading** | **Speculative**: profit from **price movements** in currencies (within **pre-set limits**), **government securities** (liquid, wholesale debt market), limited **equity** (restricted by the central bank), **credit instruments** (securitised paper, pass-through certificates, participation notes, **credit default swaps**) |

**Transfer pricing** allocates the **cost of funds** to departments rationally, adds the **cost of hedging** and gives Treasury a small **margin as funding centre**. Banks also use **RAROC** (risk adjusted return on capital) pricing. **Trading carries market risk**, so strict **risk controls** apply.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A product with a built-in spread earns even if the customer does not move the market.

payload.title: Swap-based arbitrage: annualised premium and gain
payload.core_explanation_md:
For a **buy/sell USD/INR swap**: the bank **buys dollars spot** and **sells forward**; the forward premium earned is **(forward - spot) / spot**.

**Annualised swap yield = (forward - spot) / spot x (365 / days).**

**Total return = swap yield + return on the dollars placed abroad.**

**Arbitrage gain = total return - rupee money market rate.**

Example pattern: spot **80.00**, 7-day forward **80.07**, dollars placed at **0.20 per cent**, rupee rate **3.50 per cent**: yield **(0.07 / 80) x (365 / 7) = 4.56 per cent**; total **4.76**; gain **1.26 per cent**.

assumptions: Both legs cover the same period
Counterparty and settlement risk are ignored
common_errors: Using a different number of days for the legs

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The gain is positive when the swap route pays more than lending rupees directly.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the swap premium annualised?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is multiplied by 365 divided by the number of days of the swap.

payload.title: Organisation of Treasury
payload.core_explanation_md:
Treasury may be a **department of head office** or a **specialised branch**.

| | Specialised branch | Head office department |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Books** | Own **P&L and general ledger** | Part of head office books |
| **Authority** | Can act as **authorised dealer** in forex and join **clearing and settlement** | Acts **only through a branch** |
| **Strength** | Autonomy | **Easier coordination** with head office departments |

The **specialised branch** is the **preferred form** for integrated treasury.

Treasury is led by a **senior head** (GM or Chief Treasury Officer) reporting to the **CFO or CEO**. Its three divisions: the **dealing room (front office)**, the **back office (treasury administration)** and the **mid-office (risk management)**, plus an **investment department** for primary issues and administrative units (accounts, systems, remittances).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A branch can hold its own accounts and act as dealer, which a department cannot.

self_check.prompt_text: Which form of organisation is preferred for an integrated treasury?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A specialised branch.

| **Back office** | **Verifies and settles** deals from **dealer slips** and **independent counterparty confirmations**; reconciles **nostro**, funding and security and **demat** accounts; ensures **margin** at the clearing corporation; **book-keeping and returns**; settlement on **value date** matters since delay harms **reputation** |

items.title: The concept of Treasury
items.core_explanation_md:
**Traditional Treasury** was a **funds management** function: keep **adequate cash balances**, **deploy surplus funds**, **source funds to bridge gaps**, and meet **reserve requirements** (the **CRR** with the central bank and, as required, **SLR** securities). It was seen as a **service and compliance centre**.

Since the **1990s reforms and deregulation**, Treasury has also become a **profit centre** with **proprietary trading and investment**, accessing markets to **lend, borrow, invest and trade**.

- **Market risk** for the whole bank is now managed by Treasury.
- It plays an active role in **asset-liability management (ALM)** and advises on **internal pricing and strategy**.
- **Investment in securities** and **foreign exchange** were once separate departments; they are now part of an **integrated Treasury**.
- Treasury mainly handles **short-term funds flow (under one year)**, though some SLR securities are held longer; **risk management** covers **all maturities**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve compliance remains a core duty even as profit-making has grown.

self_check.prompt_text: What was the traditional role of bank Treasury?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Funds management: keeping adequate cash, deploying surplus funds, bridging gaps and meeting reserve requirements.

items.title: Integrated Treasury and why it emerged
items.core_explanation_md:
**Integrated Treasury** joins the **money market, securities market and foreign exchange** operations. It followed **financial sector reforms**: **deregulated interest rates** and a **rupee that is convertible on current account** and, to a large extent, capital account.

**Why it matters:**

- Banks can shift funds across **currency markets** for **interest arbitrage** (for example placing in rupee commercial paper while lending dollars in the global inter-bank market).
- **Rupee and foreign currency cash flows are no longer separate**: one **integrated cash flow** is the basis.
- **Developed domestic markets and settlement systems** let funds move **between long and short term** or **between currencies**.
- Trading in many currencies creates **currency and interest rate risk**, together **market risk**, so Treasury runs **risk management and derivatives**.
- Corporates now deal with Treasury directly for **hedging export receivables**, **foreign currency loans** and **overseas investment** (**merchant business**).

**Driving forces:** **integrated cash flow management**, **interest arbitrage**, **access to global resources**, **corporate demand for high-end services**, **risk management**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Integration turns separate currency desks into one view of cash and risk.

self_check.prompt_text: What is merchant business in treasury?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Treasury transactions with customers, as distinct from the bank own trading and investment business.

items.title: Globalisation and capital flows
items.core_explanation_md:
**Globalisation** is the **integration of the domestic market with global markets**, with **free capital flows** and **minimum regulatory intervention**.

**Forms of capital flow:** **portfolio investment** (equity and debt), **direct investment** (plants, projects, outsourcing), **external commercial borrowings**, **equity or debt issued in global markets**, **mergers and acquisitions**, and **payments for technology, royalties and services**.

**Benefits and risks:** inflows **supplement domestic resources**, but **sudden swings in portfolio flows** can raise **volatility** of share prices, interest rates and exchange rates and bring **systemic risk** from other countries (the late 1990s East Asian crisis is the courseware example).

**Controls in India (principles):** foreign exchange transactions go by **automatic route through authorised dealers** or by **approval of the central bank**; **current account** is largely liberal and most **capital** flows are by automatic route, but **full capital account convertibility is not permitted**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Capital account openness is kept partial because unrestricted flows can destabilise the economy.

items.title: Impact of globalisation on treasury activity
items.core_explanation_md:
**First: interest and exchange rates.** Domestic rates are influenced by **global rates** through **cross-border flows**; these flows also affect exchange rates. India has a **managed float**; in an open economy the exchange rate also depends on **relative inflation, interest rates, GDP growth, stock markets and commodity prices**.

**Second: new institutional structure.** **Regulators, clearing and settlement bodies, depositories, credit information bureaus and rating agencies**, plus **primary dealers, mutual funds and institutions**, **deepen markets** and **reduce counterparty risk**.

**Third: derivatives.** **Rupee derivatives** (**swaps, forwards, options**) were allowed in phases; later **currency and interest rate futures, credit default swaps** and **exchange-traded options**. **Equity derivatives** are popular with investors but **banks have not been permitted** to use them (courseware). Dates and limits are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Derivatives let Treasury hedge as well as trade.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Global influence on interest and exchange rates, new institutional structure and rupee derivatives.

items.title: Treasury as a profit centre: reasons and conventional sources
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why Treasury profits are attractive:**

1. It operates in **inter-bank markets** with **almost no credit risk**, so it needs **little capital** (though **market risk** capital still applies and **institutional credit risk** has become significant).
2. It is **highly leveraged**, so the **return on capital** can be high.
3. **Operating costs are low**: **few specialist staff** do **high-value** deals in **narrow spreads**, so profit comes from **volume**.

**Conventional sources of profit:**

| Source | How it earns |
| --- | --- |
| **Foreign exchange business** | **Buy-sell spread** to customers; residual position **squared in the inter-bank market**; an **overbought or oversold (open) position** at day end carries **exchange risk** |
| **Money market deals** | Earlier **lending surplus** and **borrowing as needed**; a **transfer pricing mechanism** gives Treasury its **cost of funds** from branches |
| **Investment** | Mostly **government securities for SLR**; other investments were secondary |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Low capital and high turnover give a high return on capital but not zero risk.

self_check.expected_takeaway: A residual overbought or oversold foreign currency position left at the end of the day, which carries exchange risk.

items.title: Contemporary sources of treasury profit
items.core_explanation_md:
Profits now come from **market operations with a proprietary position**:

| Source | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Interest arbitrage** | Exploit **interest differentials** across currency and security markets (borrow USD and lend rupees, or the reverse; borrow in money market and invest in **commercial paper or T-bills**; arbitrage between **OTC and futures** markets) |
| **Trading** | **Speculative**: profit from **price movements** in currencies (within **pre-set limits**), **government securities** (liquid, wholesale debt market), limited **equity** (restricted by the central bank), **credit instruments** (securitised paper, pass-through certificates, participation notes, **credit default swaps**) |
| **Treasury products** | **Derivatives and structured products** for corporates, for example a **forward rate agreement** to fix a rate on future commercial paper, or a **swap** turning a **floating dollar loan into fixed-rate rupee interest**, each with a **buy-sell spread** in the bank favour |

**Transfer pricing** allocates the **cost of funds** to departments rationally, adds the **cost of hedging** and gives Treasury a small **margin as funding centre**. Banks also use **RAROC** (risk adjusted return on capital) pricing. **Trading carries market risk**, so strict **risk controls** apply.

items.title: Swap-based arbitrage: annualised premium and gain
items.core_explanation_md:
For a **buy/sell USD/INR swap**: the bank **buys dollars spot** and **sells forward**; the forward premium earned is **(forward - spot) / spot**.

**Annualised swap yield = (forward - spot) / spot x (365 / days).**

**Total return = swap yield + return on the dollars placed abroad.**

**Arbitrage gain = total return - rupee money market rate.**

Example pattern: spot **80.00**, 7-day forward **80.07**, dollars placed at **0.20 per cent**, rupee rate **3.50 per cent**: yield **(0.07 / 80) x (365 / 7) = 4.56 per cent**; total **4.76**; gain **1.26 per cent**.

assumptions: Both legs cover the same period
Counterparty and settlement risk are ignored
common_errors: Using a different number of days for the legs

items.expanded_explanation_md: The gain is positive when the swap route pays more than lending rupees directly.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the swap premium annualised?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is multiplied by 365 divided by the number of days of the swap.

items.title: Organisation of Treasury
items.core_explanation_md:
Treasury may be a **department of head office** or a **specialised branch**.

| | Specialised branch | Head office department |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Books** | Own **P&L and general ledger** | Part of head office books |
| **Authority** | Can act as **authorised dealer** in forex and join **clearing and settlement** | Acts **only through a branch** |
| **Strength** | Autonomy | **Easier coordination** with head office departments |

The **specialised branch** is the **preferred form** for integrated treasury.

Treasury is led by a **senior head** (GM or Chief Treasury Officer) reporting to the **CFO or CEO**. Its three divisions: the **dealing room (front office)**, the **back office (treasury administration)** and the **mid-office (risk management)**, plus an **investment department** for primary issues and administrative units (accounts, systems, remittances).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A branch can hold its own accounts and act as dealer, which a department cannot.

items.title: Front office, back office and mid-office

| **Front office (dealing room)** | Headed by a **Chief Dealer**; dealers **specialise** in forex, money or securities markets; **execute deals only**; **no part in settlement**; may include **merchant desk** and **ALM desk** |
| **Back office** | **Verifies and settles** deals from **dealer slips** and **independent counterparty confirmations**; reconciles **nostro**, funding and security and **demat** accounts; ensures **margin** at the clearing corporation; **book-keeping and returns**; settlement on **value date** matters since delay harms **reputation** |

| **Investment department** | **Primary issues** of corporate debt: **credit appraisal and documentation**; decisions by an **investment committee** |
